```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
# results and settings of the installed reproduction and validation scripts
read_results <- function(folder, name) {
  read.csv(system.file(folder, "results", name, package = "bssd",
                       mustWork = TRUE), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
# value assigned at the top level of an installed validation script
script_value <- function(script, name) {
  exprs <- parse(system.file("validation", script, package = "bssd",
                             mustWork = TRUE))
  for (e in exprs) {
    if (is.call(e) && identical(e[[1L]], as.name("<-")) &&
        identical(e[[2L]], as.name(name))) {
      return(eval(e[[3L]], baseenv()))
    }
  }
  stop("'", name, "' is not assigned in ", script, call. = FALSE)
}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
fmt_e <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
fmt_n <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
# MCMC comparisons of a validation script. The tolerance of each item is four
# Monte Carlo standard errors. For the median, the reference is 0.5 and the
# compared value is the MCMC proportion of draws below the bssd median.
mcmc_table <- function(v, rr = "r") {
  v <- v[v$judgement != "INFO", ]
  stat <- sub("^.*_", "", v$id)
  med <- stat == "MED"
  quantity <- stat
  is_p <- grepl("^P[0-9]", stat)
  quantity[is_p] <- sprintf("P(%s > %s)", rr, sub("^P", "", stat[is_p]))
  quantity[stat == "PROB"] <- sub(" [|] data[)].*$", ")",
                                  v$quantity[stat == "PROB"])
  quantity[med] <- sprintf("P(%s <= bssd median)", rr)
  quantity[stat == "MEAN"] <- sprintf("mean of %s", rr)
  quantity[stat == "IPP"] <- "placebo incidence"
  quantity[stat == "IPD"] <- "study drug incidence"
  bssd_value <- ifelse(med, v$reference, v$bssd)
  mcmc_value <- ifelse(med, v$bssd, v$reference)
  data.frame(data = sub("^[A-Z]+_([A-Z][0-9]+)_.*$", "\\1", v$id),
             quantity = quantity, bssd = bssd_value, mcmc = mcmc_value,
             difference = bssd_value - mcmc_value, se = v$tolerance / 4,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
show_mcmc <- function(m) {
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Data = m$data, Quantity = m$quantity,
                          bssd = fmt(m$bssd), MCMC = fmt(m$mcmc),
                          Difference = fmt_e(m$difference),
                          SE = fmt_e(m$se),
                          Ratio = fmt(abs(m$difference) / m$se, 2)),
               align = "llrrrrr")
}
# effective sample sizes of the posterior probabilities P(r > c)
ess_range <- function(v) {
  note <- v$note[grepl("_(PROB|P[0-9.]+)$", v$id)]
  range(as.numeric(sub("^.*ESS ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1", note)))
}
# comparison of the default integration grid with a finer grid or with the
# Python reference (validate_convergence.R)
show_convergence <- function(v) {
  parts <- regmatches(v$quantity, regexec(paste0(
    "^(.*), (finer grid vs default|Python reference vs default|",
    "Python reference vs finer grid), (.*)$"), v$quantity))
  parts <- do.call(rbind, parts)
  err <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("^reported error ", "", v$note)))
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Data = parts[, 4], Comparison = parts[, 3],
                          Quantity = sub(" [|] data[)]$", ")", parts[, 2]),
                          Reference = fmt(v$reference, 6),
                          bssd = fmt(v$bssd, 6),
                          Difference = fmt_e(v$abs_diff),
                          `Error estimate` = ifelse(is.na(err), "",
                                                    fmt_e(err)),
                          check.names = FALSE),
               align = "lllrrrr")
}
```

## Model

The log-logistic Bernoulli (LL_BERN) model of Duncan (2026, Section 3.4)
replaces the exponential distribution of EXP_BERN (`vignette("expbern")`) by
the log-logistic distribution, so that the hazard of the event can change
over time. For subject $i$ with the follow-up time $t_i$, the event indicator
$Y_i$ follows
$$P(Y_i = 1) = w_p F(t_i; \mu_p, \sigma_p) + w_d F(t_i; \mu_d, \sigma_d), \quad F(t; \mu, \sigma) = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + \exp\{(\log t - \mu) / \sigma\}},$$
where $w_p = 1 / (k + 1)$ and $w_d = k / (k + 1)$ for the randomization ratio
$k:1$, and $(\mu_p, \sigma_p)$ and $(\mu_d, \sigma_d)$ are the location and
scale parameters on placebo and on the study drug. The hazard is decreasing
when $\sigma \ge 1$ and first increases and then decreases when
$\sigma < 1$. With the values $\mu$ and $\sigma$ estimated from historical
placebo data, the priors are
$$\mu_p \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(PT_{HP} \mu / DF_p, PT_{HP} / DF_p), \quad \sigma_p \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(PT_{HP} \sigma / DF_p, PT_{HP} / DF_p),$$
$$\mu_d \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\mu, 1), \quad \sigma_d \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\sigma, 1),$$
with the shape and rate parameterization. The priors of the placebo
parameters have the means $\mu$ and $\sigma$, and $PT_{HP} / DF_p$ sets their
precision; the priors of the study drug parameters are weakly informative.

Duncan (2026) does not state which relative risk is used for the signal
criterion of this model. bssd uses the ratio of the cumulative incidences at
a time $t^*$,
$$RR(t^*) = F(t^*; \mu_d, \sigma_d) / F(t^*; \mu_p, \sigma_p),$$
and declares a signal when
$P\{RR(t^*) > \theta_c \mid \mathrm{data}\} > P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}$.

The arguments of `llbern_post()` correspond to the symbols as follows.

| Symbol | Argument | Description |
|---|---|---|
| $Y_i$ | `y` | event indicator of each subject (1 if the subject had the event during follow-up) |
| $t_i$ | `t` | follow-up time of each subject |
| $k$ | `k` | randomization ratio of study drug to placebo |
| $\mu$, $\sigma$ | `mu_hp`, `sigma_hp` | log-logistic parameters estimated from the historical placebo data |
| $PT_{HP}$ | `pt_hp` | total patient time of the historical placebo data |
| $DF_p$ | `df_p` | discount factor |
| | `mu_d_prior`, `sigma_d_prior` | shape and rate of the priors of $\mu_d$ and $\sigma_d$ (defaults `r deparse(formals(llbern_post)$mu_d_prior)` and `r deparse(formals(llbern_post)$sigma_d_prior)`) |
| $t^*$ | `t_star` | time at which the relative risk and the cumulative incidences are evaluated |
| $\theta_c$ | `rr0` | critical value of $RR(t^*)$ (default `r formals(llbern_post)$rr0`) |
| $P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}$ | `cutoff` | posterior probability threshold (default `r formals(llbern_post)$cutoff`) |

The parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ refer to the time unit of `t` and
`t_star`. `ll_cdf()` computes $F(t; \mu, \sigma)$, and `ll_mu()` gives the
location parameter for a cumulative incidence at a given time.

## Example

The following data are simulated with `sim_blinded()`: 150 subjects
randomized 1:1 with uniform entry over 26 weeks, up to 104 weeks of
follow-up, and log-logistic times to the event with $\sigma = 0.8$. The
cumulative incidence at week 104 is
`r fmt(100 * ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8), 1)`% on placebo
($\mu_p = 7.3$) and 12% on the study drug, whose location parameter is
obtained with `ll_mu()`. The blinded analysis is at week 117.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)
mu_d <- ll_mu(0.12, t = 104, sigma = 0.8)
mu_d
d <- sim_blinded(n = 150, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 104,
                 analysis_time = 117, dist = "loglogistic",
                 par_p = c(7.3, 0.8), par_d = c(mu_d, 0.8))
c(subjects = nrow(d), events = sum(d$event))
```

The priors use the placebo parameters as `mu_hp` and `sigma_hp`, and a
historical placebo group of 75 subjects followed for 104 weeks
(150 patient-years) discounted by $DF_p = 2$, as in the simulations in the
folder `reproduce` of the installed package. The relative risk is evaluated
at the end of follow-up, $t^* = 104$ weeks.

```{r fit}
fit <- llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
                   sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = 75 * 104 / 52, df_p = 2,
                   t_star = 104)
fit
summary(fit)
```

The posterior probabilities for other critical values of $RR(104)$ are
obtained with `rr0`; `details = FALSE` skips the quantiles and
`control = list(check = FALSE)` skips the repeated computation for the error
estimate:

```{r rr0}
vapply(c(1, 1.5, 2), function(q) {
  llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
              sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = 75 * 104 / 52, df_p = 2,
              t_star = 104, rr0 = q, details = FALSE,
              control = list(check = FALSE))$prob
}, numeric(1))
```

The posterior distribution of $RR(t^*)$ can have a heavy right tail, so the
posterior median is a more stable summary than the posterior mean.

## Numerical integration

`llbern_post()` integrates the four-dimensional posterior numerically on the
coordinates $\log \mu_p$, $\log \sigma_p$, $\log \mu_d$ and the prior
distribution function of $\sigma_d$. A coarse grid locates the region that
holds almost all posterior mass. Gauss-Legendre quadrature is used for three
coordinates and Chebyshev interpolation for $\log \mu_d$; because
$RR(t^*) > \theta_c$ holds exactly when $\mu_d$ is below a value determined
by the other three parameters, the posterior probability is obtained from the
cumulative integral of the interpolant (see `?llbern_post`). With
`control$check = TRUE`, the default, the computation is repeated on a finer
grid, the finer result is returned, and twice the absolute difference in
`prob` is reported as the error estimate (`fit$integration$error`, here
`r fmt_e(fit$integration$error)`). The factor two is explained in
`?llbern_post`: when there are few events, the error decreases slowly as the
grid is refined. The error estimate can be reduced by increasing
`control$n_inner`.

```{r convergence-data, include = FALSE}
conv <- read_results("validation", "validate_convergence.csv")
conv <- conv[grepl("^C_L", conv$id), ]
py <- conv[grepl("_PY_", conv$id), ]
```

The script `inst/validation/validate_convergence.R` compares the default
grid with a much finer grid for the following data sets. For L1, whose
posterior of $\sigma_d$ has much mass near zero, both are also compared with
an independent reference computed in Python
(`inst/validation/python/ref_llbern_breakpoints.py`). The column Error
estimate is the error estimate reported with the default grid.

```{r convergence-table, echo = FALSE}
show_convergence(conv)
```

The largest difference is `r fmt_e(max(conv$abs_diff))`, and it does not
exceed the error estimate; all `r nrow(conv)` items are
`r paste(unique(conv$judgement), collapse = ", ")`.

## Comparison with MCMC

```{r mcmc-data, include = FALSE}
jags <- read_results("validation", "validate_jags.csv")
v <- jags[grepl("^J_L", jags$id), ]
m <- mcmc_table(v, rr = "RR")
err <- v$bssd[grepl("_ERR$", v$id)]
ll_cases <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "ll_cases")
n_burn <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "n_burn")
n_iter <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "n_iter")
n_chain <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "n_chain")
model_ll <- script_value("validate_jags.R", "model_ll")
ess <- ess_range(v)
is_prob <- grepl("^P[(]", m$quantity)
pick <- function(name) vapply(ll_cases, function(cs) cs[[name]], numeric(1))
pair <- function(name) {
  vapply(ll_cases, function(cs) sprintf("(%g, %g)", cs[[name]][1L],
                                        cs[[name]][2L]), character(1))
}
incidence <- function(name) {
  vapply(ll_cases, function(cs) {
    sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ll_cdf(cs$follow_up, cs[[name]][1L],
                                   cs[[name]][2L]))
  }, character(1))
}
ids <- vapply(ll_cases, function(cs) cs$id, character(1))
prob_rows <- v[grepl("_PROB$", v$id), ]
events <- sub("^.*events = ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1", prob_rows$quantity)
names(events) <- sub("^J_(L[0-9]+)_PROB$", "\\1", prob_rows$id)
```

The script `inst/validation/validate_jags.R` compares `llbern_post()` with
MCMC in JAGS for the simulated data sets below. The JAGS model is written
directly from the model specification of Duncan (2026, Section 3.4) and
shares no code with bssd:

```{r jags-model, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
cat(trimws(model_ll), "\n")
```

The results in this section are read from the output of that script
(`validate_jags.csv` in the folder `validation/results` of the installed
package); JAGS is not run when this article is built.

```{r mcmc-settings, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Data = ids, N = pick("n"), k = pick("k"), Events = unname(events[ids]),
  `Placebo (mu, sigma)` = pair("par_p"),
  `Study drug (mu, sigma)` = pair("par_d"),
  `Incidences at t*` = paste(incidence("par_p"), incidence("par_d"),
                             sep = " / "),
  `t* (week)` = pick("follow_up"),
  `Analysis (week)` = round(pick("tau"), 1),
  `Prior (mu_hp, sigma_hp)` = pair("prior"), rr0 = pick("rr0"),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

The data are simulated with `sim_blinded()` with the placebo and study drug
parameters, and the relative risk and the incidences are evaluated at the end
of follow-up ($t^*$); the script gives the other settings. JAGS was run with
`r n_chain` chains, `r fmt_n(n_burn)` burn-in iterations and
`r fmt_n(n_iter)` iterations per chain. The Monte Carlo standard error (SE)
of each MCMC estimate uses the effective sample size of the draws
(`coda::effectiveSize()`); for the posterior probabilities, the effective
sample sizes are between `r fmt_n(ess[1])` and `r fmt_n(ess[2])`. For the
median, the table shows the MCMC proportion of draws below the posterior
median of $RR(t^*)$ computed by bssd, which should be 0.5. The incidences are
the posterior means of the cumulative incidences at $t^*$. The column Ratio
is the absolute difference divided by the SE.

```{r mcmc-table, echo = FALSE}
show_mcmc(m)
```

In all `r nrow(m)` items, the bssd value is within
`r fmt(max(abs(m$difference) / m$se), 1)` standard errors of the MCMC value,
and `r sum(abs(m$difference) / m$se <= 2)` items are within two standard
errors. The largest absolute difference in a posterior probability is
`r fmt(max(abs(m$difference[is_prob])))`, while the SEs of the MCMC
probabilities are between `r fmt(min(m$se[is_prob]))` and
`r fmt(max(m$se[is_prob]))`. The integration error estimates of bssd for
these data sets are between `r fmt_e(min(err))` and `r fmt_e(max(err))`.
Differences of this size are expected from the Monte Carlo error of MCMC
alone, so the difference between the numerical integration of bssd and MCMC
is negligible in practice. The validation script judges an item PASS when
the difference is at most four standard errors;
`r sum(v$judgement == "PASS")` of the `r sum(v$judgement != "INFO")` compared
items are PASS.

## References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using
alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. *Journal of
Biopharmaceutical Statistics*, 36(2), 227-244.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532>
